lead: Close the book, try to say it yourself, then see what you missed.
when: When you've finished a book or course and want to check whether you really understand it, when you're getting ready to review, or when you notice you "get it" while looking but lose it once the material is gone.
body:
When you read a passage, you may feel you understand every sentence. Then you close the page, try to explain it, and suddenly can't put it clearly. That doesn't necessarily mean you're bad at learning. "It looks familiar" and "I can pull it out of memory" were never the same thing.

Retrieval practice, also called active recall, is a way of studying in which you pull previously learned information out of memory without looking at the material for the moment, then strengthen your learning by checking it and getting feedback.

Retrieval practice adds a step of pulling things out: before looking at the answer, try to explain, jot down the key points, or solve a problem, then go back to the material to check. It helps you find where something only looks familiar, and it turns the act of retrieving into part of the practice.

It doesn't have to feel like a stressful exam. Start by recalling one small section, allow yourself to leave things out, then fill in whatever you forgot or got wrong. What matters is genuinely trying to retrieve and using feedback to correct yourself, not reciting the original word for word on the first try.

A cycle diagram can separate two steps: first trying to recall without the material, then opening it to check. Use what you find to correct the next round. It's not about reading the answer while telling yourself you've already memorized it.
example:
You've just read the entry on sunk cost and think "money already spent shouldn't decide your next step" is easy. Close the page and try to answer: What counts as an investment you can't get back? Should refundable fees be taken into account? When is it still reasonable to keep going?

Write down your answers, then open the entry to check. If all you remembered was "don't stick with it," fill in what you missed: what you should compare are the benefits and costs from now on, and if something still has future value, it can make sense to continue. A few days later, explain it again using a different everyday example. That tests your understanding far better than staring at one familiar sentence.
extra:
You're learning a work procedure, and rereading the instructions makes it feel very familiar. In a safe practice setting, close the instructions, write out the key steps first, then try to run through it once, and finally check for gaps and mistakes.

If the task involves danger or something important, don't skip the official checklist just to do it "from memory." Practicing to learn and doing the real thing have different requirements, and a checklist is still a tool for reducing mistakes.
steps: After finishing a small chunk, close the material for now and bring the content back to mind using questions, a blank page, or your own words.
Open the material again to check, pinpoint what you left out, misunderstood, or couldn't support, and correct it right away.
After some time, retrieve it again with different questions or situations, combining spaced review with application so you don't just memorize fixed answers.
caution: Retrieval practice isn't rote memorization, and it can't replace first understanding the material, getting needed explanations, and hands-on practice. If you haven't understood the content at all, go back and build the basics, then narrow the scope of your practice. Don't keep repeating mistakes you haven't checked. It's fine for practice to be a little hard, but you don't need to treat suffering as proof that learning is working.
exercise: Close this page and write, in your own words, the difference between retrieval practice and rereading, plus one thing you could practice today. Then come back, check, and fill in one thing you missed.
brief: A stick figure gently closes a book, pulls several puzzle pieces of information out of their head onto a blank sheet, then opens the book and uses a magnifying glass to check a missing piece; a light loop connects retrieving, checking, and trying again.
diagramCaption: First meet the material, then try to retrieve it without looking, then check and correct, and practice again after a while. Keep retrieving and checking separate; don't start by reading straight off the answer.
sources: UC San Diego Department of Psychology · Retrieval Practice
